_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: It teaches us another matter in passing: that it did not teach “the most attractive among the gentiles,” because it is forbidden to apply a term of beauty to a gentile, in accordance with Rav Yehuda, as it is written: “Nor show mercy to them [lo teḥonnem]” (Deuteronomy 7:2), [read as] do not grant them grace [ḥen].
rashi:a3.1: But isn’t it taught: with regard to the rapist and the seducer.
rashi:a3.2: The lowliest among the Israelites and the most prominent in the priesthood: evidently it does deal with two nations.
rashi:a4.1: With a gentile you do not find it: the law of an ancestral field, that one redeems it for fifty silver shekels and not at its value, for they are not people with ancestral holdings in Eretz Yisrael.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. Both one who consecrates: a field in the sands of the maḥoz, around a city, which is not so valuable because of the trampling of feet. Ḥulat [means] the surroundings, like “the open space [meḥol] of a vineyard” (Kilayim 4:1). (Another version:) maḥoz [means] a city. Another version: Maḥoz is the name of a place whose fields were not valuable.
rashi:a5.2: The orchards of Sebastia: the vineyards of that place, and they are of very high quality.
rashi:a5.3: Gives: whoever redeems them, whether the owner or another person, [gives] fifty silver shekels for an area for sowing a ḥomer of barley, if it was at the beginning of the Jubilee [cycle]; and if not, he deducts according to the years that have passed, a sela and a pundeyon for each year, as the verse writes.
rashi:a6.1: Both an ancestral field etc.: for all of them are redeemed for fifty shekels.
rashi:a6.2: An ancestral field: if the owner redeems it, one adds a fifth to the fifty, as it is written: “And if he that sanctified the field will redeem it” etc. (Leviticus 27:19).
rashi:a6.3: And with a purchased field one does not give a fifth: as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a7.1: Gemara. He consecrates generously: the trees by themselves and the land by itself, and not that the trees are redeemed along with the land.
rashi:a8.1: Orchards: these are planted vineyards, and it teaches fifty shekels; evidently the trees are redeemed along with the land.
rashi:a9.1: I have: [derived that it is] redeemed for fifty shekels only for an area of sowing that is suitable for sowing.
rashi:a10.1: He redeems: the trees at their value, and then he redeems the land as well. And “field, in any case,” which it says, refers only to the land.
rashi:a11.1: He consecrated three trees: planted and spread out in their proper order, at the planting density of ten to a beit se’a; that is, if ten were spread out the way these are, they would take up this beit se’a. This is the rule for planting trees, and all the land between them is needed for them. Therefore, if he consecrated them, he has consecrated the land between them and all the small trees between them.
rashi:a12.1: Less than that: if they are planted at less than the density of ten to a beit se’a, or more than that, this is not the order of planting trees, and he consecrated only the trees; and when he redeems them, he redeems them at their value.
rashi:a12.2: One after the other: the Temple treasury did not acquire land, for there is acquisition of land only with three trees [acquired together], as it says in Bava Batra.
rashi:a13.1: And not only that: and not only are these redeemed at their value, where there is no consecration of land with them at all.
rashi:a13.2: But even if he consecrated the trees: that are not planted in order.
rashi:a13.3: And afterward he consecrated land: where one could say, let them be redeemed along with their land; even so, since they were not consecrated together, he redeems the trees at their value, and the land is redeemed at fifty shekels for an area of sowing.
rashi:a14.1: A refutation of Rav Huna: from the first clause, where, when he consecrated them together, they are redeemed along with the land. [Rashi’s heading reads “a refutation of Rav Huna,” words not in the printed Gemara here.]
rashi:a15.1: Has consecrated all of it: everything in it.
rashi:a15.2: Rabbi Shimon says, he did not consecrate: the trees in it.
rashi:a15.3: Except a grafted carob and a sycamore stump: for they are old and very large and draw from the consecrated field more than other trees; and so it is explained in Bava Batra. Sycamore stump [sadan hashikma]: it is the way of sycamores to be cut so that they grow thicker; before it is cut it is called a “virgin sycamore,” and after the cutting it is called a sycamore stump. So it is taught in tractate Niddah (8b).
rashi:a17.1: Let one follow the redemption: and since at the time of redemption there is land with the trees.
rashi:a17.2: Let them be redeemed along with their land: even though at the time of consecration he consecrated them by themselves.
rashi:a18.1: And he consecrated it and afterward his father died: even though at the time of consecration it was a purchased field, since after his father died it is an ancestral field.
rashi:a18.2: From where that it should be before him as an ancestral field: and be redeemed for fifty shekels and not at its value.
rashi:a19.1: The verse states etc.: a field that is not fit to be an ancestral field has the law of a purchased field, to be redeemed at its value; this one is excluded etc.
rashi:a20.1: And afterward he consecrated it: for at the time of consecration it is an ancestral field; but if he consecrated it and afterward his father died, it is only like a purchased field.
tosafot:a4.1: With a gentile you do not find it: because they are not people with ancestral holdings. And even though we say (Kiddushin 17b) that a gentile inherits his father by Torah law, nevertheless they had no ancestral holding in the land, and this law applies only in Eretz Yisrael, for it is a mitzva dependent on the land, and a gentile has no inheritance in the land.
tosafot:a11.1: He consecrated three trees of a planting of ten to a beit se’a: these trees are saplings, for if they were grown trees, three [trees] to a beit se’a would suffice.
tosafot:a12.1: In brief: [On “less than that or more than that, he did not consecrate the land.”] At ten to a beit se’a, each tree has 250 square cubits. Tosafot ask from Bava Batra 82a (HaMokher et HaSefina): one who buys three trees standing from four to sixteen cubits apart acquires the land beneath them, between them and beside them, as far as a picker with his basket; so trees eight by eight cubits apart (64 square cubits each) are not too close, yet here less than 250 means no land. The Ri answers that a seller differs from one who consecrates, and a sale needs less. They ask further: here more than 250 means no land, while in a sale trees up to sixteen by sixteen cubits apart (256) are not too spread out; they answer that the sixteen cubits of a sale are measured as a circle, and a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, so a sale still needs less than consecration. Rabbeinu Shmuel in Bava Batra asked from a Tosefta that seller and consecrator do not differ in this, and answered that it is a dispute of tanna’im. A last difficulty: Rabbi Shimon holds there that eight cubits between trees is not too far even for consecration, yet the Gemara soon sets this baraita of ten to a beit se’a as Rabbi Shimon. They answer that it is set as Rabbi Shimon only for the rule that one consecrates sparingly, not for the measure of planting. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: The orchards of Sebastia: which in that place are of very high quality. When he redeems, he gives fifty shekels, whether for this or for that.
gershom:a2.1: [It is forbidden for a person to say: How beautiful is this gentile, because it is stated: “Nor show mercy to them” (Deuteronomy 7:2): do not grant them grace.]
gershom:a3.1: For they are not people with ancestral holdings [the editor suggests adding: in Eretz Yisrael], for a gentile does not acquire [the field itself]; and furthermore, he has no paternal kin and does not inherit his father. [The editor notes: see Kiddushin 17b, that a gentile inherits his father by Torah law, and so Tosafot here; this needs examination.]
gershom:a4.1: Mishna. In the sands of the maḥoz: that is, a field near the city’s maḥoz, which people trample; and furthermore, since it is near the city and stands with its standing grain, people see it and cast an evil eye on it, and it does not produce so much fruit.
gershom:a5.1: Gemara. He consecrates generously: and he consecrated the trees for their value [by themselves, and then he redeems the land, etc.].
gershom:a6.1: Orchards implies that it has trees, and it teaches that he gives fifty shekels [for an area of] sowing a ḥomer of barley; evidently he need not redeem the trees by themselves.
gershom:a7.1: [I meant land suitable for orchards, not land that has trees in it.]
gershom:a8.1: [The verse states] “field,” in any case: that is, that he redeems the field and need not redeem the trees.
gershom:a9.1: [Here too, he redeems and redeems again: that is, after he has redeemed the field, he redeems the trees.]
gershom:a10.1: Of a planting of ten to a beit se’a: that is, they are planted [evenly] within a beit se’a. He has consecrated the land along with the trees, even though he did not mention the land, because it is subordinate to the trees, [and the trees between them: small trees that came up between those trees]. Less than that or more than that: those ten trees are planted in less than a beit se’a, or spread over more than a beit se’a, for they have lost the status of [a planting of] trees.
gershom:a11.1: Or if he consecrated them one after the other: the trees; he has not consecrated the land.
gershom:a12.1: But [even if] he explicitly consecrated the land, and when he redeems etc. And he raises the challenge from the first clause of the baraita.
gershom:a13.1: Rabbi Shimon says: He consecrated only the carob etc.: for they are significant, since they draw from the consecrated field; but not the other trees, for one who consecrates, consecrates sparingly.
gershom:a14.1: He consecrated the trees and afterward consecrated the land: even though they are planted ten to a beit se’a, and he consecrated one after the other, [he redeems the trees at their value and then redeems again, etc.].
gershom:a15.1: [Let one follow] the redemption: since at the time of redemption the land is consecrated together with the trees, let them be redeemed along with their land.
gershom:a16.1: From where with regard to one who purchases a field from his father and consecrated it: for at the time of consecration it was a purchased field.
gershom:a17.1: And afterward his father died: and he would have been fit to inherit that field had he not bought it.
gershom:a18.1: From where that it should be before him: now, at the time of redemption.
gershom:a19.1: As an ancestral field: and he redeems an area for sowing a ḥomer of barley for fifty silver shekels.
gershom:a20.1: The verse states: “And if a field that he has bought” etc. Evidently Rabbi Shimon follows the redemption: even though it was not an ancestral field when he consecrated it, but [it is one] at the time of redemption, we go by the present.
gershom:a21.1: And his father died and afterward he consecrated it: for both at the time of consecration and at the time of redemption it is an ancestral field.
rashi:b2.1: If because of the verse: “which is not of his ancestral field”; perhaps it does not come to exclude a case where he consecrated it and afterward his father died, but rather to exclude a case where his father died and afterward he consecrated it, as Rabbi Meir expounds it.
rashi:b3.1: The redemption: and since by the time of redemption his father had died, it has become an ancestral field.
rashi:b5.1: If so: that it comes for Rabbi Meir’s ruling, let the Merciful One write etc.
rashi:b6.1: He redeems them at their value: even though they are ancestral.
rashi:b7.1: He did not redeem them: and the treasurer sold them to another.
rashi:b7.2: They go out to the priests in the Jubilee: as it is written: “And if he will not redeem” etc. (Leviticus 27:20), and it is written: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” etc. (Leviticus 27:21).
rashi:b7.3: The Merciful One said “field”: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” etc. (ibid.).
rashi:b8.1: Less than two years: even though one who sells land to another may not redeem it until it has been two years in the hand of the purchaser, as it is written: “According to the number of years of the crops” etc. (Leviticus 25:15).
rashi:b9.1: He did not redeem them, they do not go out to the priests in the Jubilee: if the treasurer sold them to another.
rashi:b11.1: Let them be redeemed along with their land: the place where the tree stands; and let them return to the owner along with their land, if he sold them and the Jubilee arrived. So why did he say: If he sold trees and did not redeem them, they do not return to the owner in the Jubilee?
rashi:b12.1: From the bottom: the place where the tree stands, down to its depths.
rashi:b12.2: Due to a claim: that he claims that [the seller] mentioned land to him.
rashi:b13.1: A purchased field: it is written: “Then the priest shall reckon for him the worth of your valuation” (Leviticus 27:23).
rashi:b13.2: Since it is stated: in the redemption of an ancestral field, “the sowing of a ḥomer of barley.”
rashi:b13.3: The verse states “worth [mikhsat]”: the count of its money, that is, its value.
rashi:b14.1: It is stated here: with a purchased field; and there: with an ancestral field.
rashi:b14.2: A fixed amount: fifty [shekels of] silver.
rashi:b15.1: Do they accept this verbal analogy: of “shall reckon,” and use it for the fifth, to derive a fifth for a purchased field from an ancestral field?
rashi:b16.1: A fifth for an ancestral field and for one who consecrates a house: in the portion of Beḥukkotai; and the fifth for a non-kosher and a kosher animal and for second tithe is also written there.
rashi:b18.1: It is taught in accordance with Rava: that there is no fifth for a purchased field.
rashi:b18.2: But not for his reason: for Rava’s reason is from the fact that [the Torah] revealed a fifth in all these places, and the baraita’s reason is that it juxtaposed it to valuations, of a person who valuated himself or another.
rashi:b19.1: Mishna. Killed a freeman, he gives his value: as it is written with regard to a forewarned ox: “If a ransom be laid on him” etc. (Exodus 21:30), and it is taught in Bava Kamma (40a): “Then he shall give for the redemption of his life”: the value of the injured party.
rashi:b19.2: Injured this one or that one: whether a slave or a freeman, and did not kill him; he pays full damage.
rashi:b20.1: Gemara. With a forewarned ox, yes; with an innocuous ox, no: this refers to the latter clause, which teaches: “injured this one or that one” etc. For the first clause is obvious to us: the fine for a slave does not apply to an innocuous ox, as it is written with regard to an innocuous ox: “But the owner of the ox shall be clear” (Exodus 21:28), and we say in Bava Kamma, in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ Arba’a VeḤamisha (42a): clear of the payment for a slave. And it also teaches: “killed a freeman, he gives his value,” and ransom does not apply to an innocuous ox, for there too we say: clear of half the ransom.
rashi:b20.2: Also an innocuous ox that injured a person etc.: in Bava Kamma, in the chapter HaMani’aḥ et HaKad: two innocuous oxen that injured each other etc.; Rabbi Akiva says: also an innocuous ox that injured a person pays full damage for the excess. That is, for the excess: if the person also injured the ox, and the court assessed the injury to the person as greater than the injury to the ox, the owner of the ox pays that excess as full damage. Evidently an innocuous ox that injured a person pays full damage.
rashi:b21.1: Since it wants to teach in the latter clause: killed a slave, killed a freeman, etc.; for this reason it chose a forewarned ox in the first clause. And what it calls “the latter clause” is not the actual latter clause, but the latter part of the first clause, for the forewarned ox is taught in the first clause.
rashi:b22.1: Mishna. Degradation: it is explained in Ketubot (40a): one assesses her by how much more a person would be willing to give for a virgin maidservant than for a non-virgin maidservant, to marry her to his slave who has given him satisfaction.
rashi:b23.1: For all matters: and he should not give her humiliation and degradation.
rashi:b24.1: One who had intercourse with a daughter of commoners etc.: as an exclamation of astonishment. But now, when he gives humiliation, there is a distinction between a daughter of kings and a daughter of commoners.
tosafot:b15.1: A dilemma was raised: do the Rabbis accept the verbal analogy and use it for the fifth, or perhaps etc.: Rabbeinu Elḥanan found it difficult: why not derive a verbal analogy from them? Granted that we do not derive a paradigm [binyan av] from them, nevertheless let us derive a verbal analogy from them. And it seems to our teacher [the text has only “R.”]: since it was necessary to write a fifth for one who consecrates an ancestral field and for one who consecrates his house, and we could have derived one from the other by a verbal analogy, yet we do not derive it, but [the Torah] wrote a fifth for each one, learn from this that they are two verses that come as one, and we do not derive from them elsewhere, even by a verbal analogy.
tosafot:b16.1: They are two verses that come as one: And if you say: what does this have to do with two verses that come as one? For with a purchased field there is a verbal analogy to derive a fifth from an ancestral field, but with one who consecrates a house there is no verbal analogy. Perhaps here, since “and he shall value” is written with one who consecrates a house, it is as if “shall reckon” were written. Or perhaps one may say that “shall reckon” is not a complete verbal analogy, even though the book calls it a verbal analogy; and we find the same in the first chapter of Bava Kamma (6b), with “field is stated above and field is stated below,” which is called a verbal analogy there, and the Ri said that it is not a complete verbal analogy. Or perhaps one may say: since “holy” is written with one who consecrates an ancestral field, and “holy” is also written with one who consecrates a house, and “holy”–“holy” is a complete verbal analogy, for this reason it calls them two verses that come as one.
tosafot:b20.1: With a forewarned ox, yes; with an innocuous, no; let us say the mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva etc.: this refers to the very last clause, which teaches: “injured this one or that one, he pays full damage.” But one cannot say that it refers to “killed a slave” and “killed a freeman,” for in this Rabbi Akiva does not disagree, that an innocuous ox pays neither ransom nor the thirty of a slave, as stated in Bava Kamma, in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ Arba’a VeḤamisha (42b).
tosafot:b22.1: Humiliation, all according to the one who humiliates and the one humiliated: and degradation is explained in Ketubot (40b): one estimates how much more a person would be willing to give for a virgin maidservant than for a non-virgin, to marry her to his slave who has given him satisfaction.
tosafot:b24.1: They will say: a daughter of kings, fifty; a daughter of a commoner, fifty: it is somewhat puzzling, for in the mishna it is taught: both the most prominent in the priesthood and the lowliest among the Israelites, he gives fifty. Why is it different, that here in the Gemara it names the prominent one as a daughter of kings, while the mishna teaches the most prominent in the priesthood?
gershom:b1.1: [What is the reason? If you think it is because of the verse that they expound, “a field that is not fit,” that] verse comes for Rabbi Meir’s ruling, for according to him it is more reasonable. [Rather, is it not that he follows the redemption?]
gershom:b2.1: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Actually, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon do not generally follow the redemption. And here, with one who purchases a field from his father, why do they follow the redemption? They found a verse and expounded it, from a superfluous verse: for if so, that we do not follow the redemption, let it write “a field that he has bought, which is not his ancestral” or “[which is not an] ancestral field”; what is “of his field”? Learn from this: [a field] that is not fit to be etc.
gershom:b3.1: Rocky ground [terashin]: a field full of rocks that is not suitable for sowing.
gershom:b4.1: Field, of any kind: whether suitable for sowing or not suitable for sowing.
gershom:b5.1: They may be redeemed in less than two years: for we say below that one who sells [his field] while the Jubilee is in force may not redeem it in less than two years, as it is stated: “According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you” (Leviticus 25:15).
gershom:b6.1: “And it shall return to his ancestral holding”: and his ancestral holding is whatever it is.
gershom:b7.1: They do not go out to the priests in the Jubilee: like an ancestral field; rather, the owner may always redeem it.
gershom:b8.1: Let them be redeemed along with their land: the trees [that he consecrated], [at an area for sowing a ḥomer of barley for fifty shekels; and let them return to the owner in the Jubilee along with their land, where he sold them]. [The editor suggests reading: the trees that he consecrated, to be redeemed by the reckoning of the sowing of a ḥomer of barley, etc.]
gershom:b9.1: From the bottom to the depths: its bottom is its base around its roots, and downward to the depths.
gershom:b10.1: [When the Nehardeans said this,] it was where he comes due to a claim: when he claims that he bought the land, the place where the tree stands, [with it], and he already has the years of presumptive ownership.
gershom:b11.1: [What does “worth [mikhsat]” teach? For it is written with a purchased field: “Then the priest shall reckon for him the worth of your valuation.”] The verse states “worth,” and “worth” means nothing but money, the money of its value, as we said below.
gershom:b12.1: [It is stated here “shall reckon,” and it is stated there, with an ancestral field: “Then the priest shall reckon for him the money according to the years” etc. Just as there it is a fixed amount, the sowing of a ḥomer of barley for fifty shekels, so too here.]
gershom:b13.1: According to the Rabbis, who say that with a purchased field one gives its value: do they accept the verbal analogy “shall reckon”–“shall reckon,” and use the verbal analogy for the fifth: just as with an ancestral field one adds a fifth, so with a purchased field one adds a fifth?
gershom:b14.1: Or perhaps they do not accept the verbal analogy, and they do not hold of a fifth [with a purchased field]?
gershom:b15.1: They are many: verses that come as one, and they do not teach.
gershom:b16.1: [“Worth [mikhsat]” means nothing but money: that is, he gives its value.] [The editor notes that this is Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading of the baraita here.]
gershom:b17.1: “And levy a tribute [mekhes] to the Lord” (Numbers 31:28): that he would fairly give one soul out of five hundred, and would not lose by it.
gershom:b18.1: Just as valuations: valuations of a person, [one does not add a fifth].
gershom:b19.1: [Killed a freeman,] he gives his value: [the value] of the owner of the ox, and that is the ransom; [and if you should] say the value of the one killed, that is money, as we say in Bava Kamma.
gershom:b20.1: Injured this one or that one: if a forewarned ox injured either a slave or a freeman, he pays full damage.
gershom:b21.1: With a forewarned ox, yes; with an innocuous ox, no: that is, a forewarned ox pays full damage if it injured a person, but an innocuous one pays only half damage.
gershom:b22.1: [Pays] for the excess: whoever injured the other more.
gershom:b23.1: Which you find with a forewarned ox: that the owner pays ransom.
gershom:b24.1: With an innocuous ox you do not find it: as it is written: “But the owner of the ox shall be clear” (Exodus 21:28).
gershom:b25.1: [All according to] the one who humiliates and the one humiliated: for if he humiliated an important person, he does not pay the same as if he humiliated a commoner; alternatively, [where] an important person humiliated, he pays more than [where] commoners humiliated.
gershom:b26.1: [But say: why? Fifty sela for all matters: for the fine, for humiliation and for degradation.]
gershom:b27.1: [If so, people will say: one who had intercourse etc.; what is the difference between this one and that one? Rather, learn from this that for the daughter of important people he adds her humiliation.]
gershom:b28.1: If so, with a slave too people will say etc. And we hold that for this one and for that one it is thirty and no more.
